title: What is agentic coding?
text:
Until recently, using an LLM meant typing into a chat box and copy-pasting the answer back into your editor. That works, but it puts you in the loop for every small action: copy this, paste here, run it, paste the error back, ask again. “Agentic coding” tools cut that loop. You give the model direct access to your project — it can read files, edit them, run code, see the output, and decide what to do next. You stay in the loop for direction and review, not for clerical handoffs.
That is the whole shift.

title: What is agentic coding?
text:
A concrete contrast






Chat-style (what you might be doing now)

You: “Write me a Stata loop that runs a regression for each year and stores coefficients.”
LLM: (gives a snippet)
You: (paste into Stata, hit run, get an error about a missing variable)
You: “I got this error: variable wage_resid not found”
LLM: (apologizes, gives a new snippet)
You: (paste, run, repeat 3 more times)










Agentic (what Claude Code does)

You: “Write a loop that runs my main regression for each year and stores the coefficients. Look at analysis.do to see how I’ve set up the covariates.”
Claude Code: (reads analysis.do, writes the loop, runs it, sees the wage_resid not found error, reads 02-build-vars.do, notices that wage_resid is generated only when a flag is set, fixes the loop, runs it again, shows you the diff and the resulting coefficients)




The chat version takes ten minutes of attention. The agentic version takes ten minutes of clock time but maybe one minute of yours.

title: What is agentic coding?
section: What you give up, and what you keep
text:
What you give up, and what you keep
You give up the moment-by-moment control of every keystroke. You can’t inspect the model’s reasoning step by step in real time, and you have to trust that it’s editing the right files in the right way.
You keep — and must exercise — direction and review. You decide what to ask for. You read the diff before accepting it. You run the regression yourself before believing the number. See verifying output.

title: What is agentic coding?
section: Why this matters for an economist specifically
text:
Why this matters for an economist specifically
It lands harder in our field than most:

Our work is heavy on small, tedious code. Renaming variables across a dozen .do files, regenerating tables in a different format, fixing a bibtex file with 200 entries — these are exactly the kinds of jobs where the agentic loop pays off.
Reproducibility matters. The model can read your whole replication package and tell you what’s missing or what won’t run on a fresh machine. A human RA would take a day; the model takes minutes.
You probably have several projects in different languages. The same tool works on Stata, R, Python, Matlab, Julia, LaTeX, and shell scripts — you don’t need to learn a different assistant for each.

title: What is agentic coding?
section: What changes for your research workflow
text:
What changes for your research workflow
What changes:

Tedious code (variable renaming, table reformatting, replication-package cleanup, .bib fixes) takes minutes instead of hours.
You stop avoiding small-but-annoying improvements (“I’ll fix that figure formatting later”) because the friction drops to near zero.
A second pair of eyes is always available: “what’s wrong with this regression specification?” gets a useful answer in seconds.
Onboarding to an unfamiliar codebase — your old paper from five years ago, a coauthor’s repo, a published replication package — gets much faster.

What does not change:

Your responsibility for the specification, identification, and interpretation. The model can suggest; you decide.
The need to read the diff before accepting code into your project.
The need to run the regression yourself before believing the number in your table.
Your research taste — what’s interesting, what’s worth doing. The model has none of it, and will happily help you do bad work efficiently.

title: Building your own skills
text:
Contrary to the impression you might get online, I don’t use many skills. The three below are simply the tasks I found myself doing over and over, the same way each time — so I wrote them down. The reason to build a skill is repetition: a task you do the same way more than twice. If you’re not repeating something, you don’t need one.
A skill is a reusable instruction set you can invoke by name. Instead of re-typing the same multi-step prompt every time (“scaffold a Pluto notebook with sliders, estimation, and identification diagnostics…”), you write it down once as a SKILL.md file and call it with /your-skill.
Mechanically, a skill is just a folder with a SKILL.md inside it:
The file has a short YAML header (the “frontmatter”) and a body. The body is the prompt Claude runs when you invoke the skill; the header tells Claude what the skill is for and how it’s allowed to run.
I keep mine in a small public repo, myccskills, with three skills in it. They’re worth walking through because they show two different shapes a useful skill can take.

title: Building your own skills
text:
The three skills

/plutonb — a knowledge skill
What it does: scaffolds a Pluto.jl notebook for a structural-econometrics simulation — model primitives as a struct, a data generating process with explicit seeds, MLE/GMM estimation with a true-vs-estimated comparison table, interactive @bind sliders, identification diagnostics, and a LaTeX appendix. You call it with a model description: /plutonb a Roy model of occupational choice.
How it’s built: it’s essentially my “how I want a structural notebook built” knowledge, written down. The body is a long, structured set of instructions — cell order, parameter-transformation conventions (exp() for variances, tanh() for correlations), how to document exclusion restrictions, a quality checklist. The frontmatter passes the model description in via $ARGUMENTS:
---
name: plutonb
description: Create a Pluto.jl notebook for structural econometrics
  simulations. Use when the user asks to create a Pluto notebook,
  simulation notebook, or structural model notebook.
user-invocable: true
allowed-tools: Bash, Read, Write, Edit, Glob, Grep
argument-hint: "[model-name-or-description]"
---
This is the most common kind of skill to write first: take a task you do repeatedly and do a particular way, and encode that way once.


/evolution — a context-gathering skill
What it does: reads a project’s git history and tells the story of how it evolved — phases, milestones, pivots, and what’s being worked on now. Run it in any repo with /evolution, or scope it (/evolution 20, /evolution 2025-01).
How it’s built: this one demonstrates two features beyond a plain prompt. First, it pre-loads context by running shell commands with the ! prefix — the output is injected into the prompt before Claude starts:
### Full git log with file-level changes
!`git log --stat --all --date=short --format="%h %ad %s" | head -500`
Second, the frontmatter runs it in a separate, read-only sub-agent so it doesn’t clutter your main session:
context: fork
agent: Explore
allowed-tools: Bash, Read, Glob, Grep
The body is then just instructions for turning that git history into a readable narrative.


/remind — also context-gathering
What it does: a snapshot of where a project stands when you come back to it after time away — branch and remote status, uncommitted work, recent commits, structure, and any saved context from CLAUDE.md / MEMORY.md.
How it’s built: same shape as /evolution — !-prefixed commands pre-load git status, the branch list, recent commits, and the directory listing, then a forked Explore agent reads CLAUDE.md and MEMORY.md and summarizes. It’s a good template to copy when you want a “gather some state, then summarize it” skill.

title: Building your own skills
section: The building blocks, in one place
text:
The building blocks, in one place
Everything above is assembled from a small set of pieces:







Piece
What it does




SKILL.md in a named folder
The skill itself; the folder name is the default skill name


name, description
The description is what Claude matches on to decide the skill applies — write it carefully


user-invocable: true
Lets you call it explicitly with /name


allowed-tools:
Restricts which tools the skill may use


argument-hint:
Documents what to pass after the name


$ARGUMENTS (in the body)
Where your input gets substituted


!`command` (in the body)
Runs a shell command and injects its output before Claude starts


context: fork + agent: Explore
Runs the skill in a separate read-only sub-agent



The two shapes worth knowing: knowledge skills (/plutonb) that encode “the way I do X,” and context skills (/evolution, /remind) that gather state with ! commands and then reason over it.

title: Building your own skills
text:
Installing them
Claude Code reads personal skills from ~/.claude/skills/. There are two ways to get mine onto your machine.
Option A — copy the skills you want. Simplest, and it won’t disturb any skills you already have:
git clone https://github.com/moshialam/myccskills.git
cp -R myccskills/plutonb ~/.claude/skills/      # repeat for evolution, remind
Option B — symlink the whole repo. This is how I run them, so my edits stay under version control. Only do this if ~/.claude/skills isn’t already holding skills of your own, since it points the entire directory at the repo:
git clone https://github.com/moshialam/myccskills.git
ln -sfn "$(pwd)/myccskills" ~/.claude/skills
Either way, verify with ls ~/.claude/skills and then, inside Claude Code, type / to confirm plutonb, evolution, and remind show up.






Note



To scope a skill to a single project instead of your whole machine, put it in .claude/skills/ inside that project’s folder rather than in ~/.claude/skills/. Project skills are a good way to share a skill with coauthors through the project’s own git repo.

title: Building your own skills
text:
Writing your own
The fastest way to start is to copy one of these as a template and edit it:

Repetitive task you do a specific way → copy plutonb, replace the body with your instructions, update name/description/argument-hint.
“Gather some state, then summarize” → copy remind, swap the ! commands for whatever you want pre-loaded.

Good candidates from elsewhere on this site: a /audit-replication skill built from the replication-package walkthrough, or a /reorganize-project skill from the messy-project walkthrough. Once you’ve done either of those by hand twice, it’s worth writing down.
See also Memory, CLAUDE.md, skills for how skills sit alongside the other ways of giving Claude persistent context.

title: How to ask
text:
The habits

Orientation pass first. Before asking for changes, ask Claude to read the project and summarize. Cheap; saves rework.
Separate audit from action. “Tell me what you’d change. Don’t change it yet.” — almost always the right first prompt for non-trivial tasks.
Be explicit about what to leave alone. “Don’t introduce new arguments. Don’t change numbers. Don’t reformat unrelated code.” Saying it costs nothing; not saying it costs a careful re-read.
Use plan mode for multi-file work. Shift+Tab until you see “plan mode”. Claude writes a plan, you approve, then it acts.
Quote files by name. “Read paper.tex and tell me…” works better than “look at my paper”. Names are unambiguous; descriptions aren’t.
One commit per logical change. Don’t let Claude do five unrelated things in one session — each one is harder to review and harder to roll back.

title: How to ask
text:
Anti-patterns

“Make this better.” Without specifics, Claude will reformat, reorganize, and rephrase, often making it worse.
“Just trust me, run it.” For destructive operations (delete files, drop database tables, force-push), make Claude pause for explicit approval. It will by default; don’t override.
“Write a complete X from scratch.” For real research code, prefer iterative: skeleton → fill in one piece → verify → next piece.

title: Worked example — auditing a replication package
text:
The single highest-value use of agentic coding for an empirical economist is replication-package work. Whether you’re preparing a package for submission, refereeing one, or trying to run a coauthor’s old project on a fresh machine, the pattern is the same: someone has to read every file, trace dependencies, and figure out why the master script breaks on line 237. Claude Code is unusually good at this.
This page walks through both directions: auditing a package you’ve inherited or are refereeing, and building one from your own working project for journal submission.

title: Worked example — auditing a replication package
text:
Setup
cd ~/Dropbox/Projects/wage-paper-replication
claude
Same orientation pass as always:

“Read the project. List every file. For each subfolder, tell me what it appears to contain. Identify any ‘master’ script — something a user would run to reproduce the results.”

title: Worked example — auditing a replication package
section: Direction A — auditing an existing package
text:
Direction A — auditing an existing package

Step 1 — produce a dependency map

“I want a dependency map of this replication package. Trace which scripts read which raw data files, which scripts produce which intermediate data files, which intermediate files are inputs to which analysis scripts, and which analysis scripts produce which tables/figures in the paper. Output as a Markdown list. Don’t run anything yet.”

This is the kind of task that takes a careful human a full day. Claude will do it in a few minutes, and it will catch things like “table_3.do reads clean_data_v2.dta but no script in the package produces clean_data_v2.dta — only clean_data_v3.dta.” That’s the bug you’re hunting for.


Step 2 — identify what’s missing

“Based on the dependency map, list everything required to reproduce this paper that is not in the package: missing raw data files, missing intermediate files that no script produces, packages or libraries used in the code but not declared, hard-coded paths that point outside the package.”

Claude will give you a clean punch list. Common findings:

A path like /Users/coauthor/Dropbox/... hardcoded into a .do file.
A library(haven) call without haven declared in a requirements.R or renv.lock.
A merge step that requires a file you got from the IRB and didn’t put in the package.



Step 3 — try to actually run it

“Try to run the master script. If you hit an error, stop, tell me what happened, and propose a minimal fix. Don’t auto-fix anything — just propose.”

This is the test that matters. A package that “should run” and a package that runs on a clean machine are different things. Claude is patient about this loop in a way humans are not.






Warning



For Stata, R, etc., Claude can call out to your installed interpreter. Make sure you’re running in the right environment — the same Stata version your coauthor used, the same R packages, etc. If you’re refereeing, this is part of the audit: the package should declare its environment.




Step 4 — document the gaps

“Write a REVIEW.md that lists everything I’d ask the authors to fix before this package is ready for publication. Group by severity: blockers (won’t run at all), important (runs but doesn’t reproduce a result), minor (style/clarity).”

You now have your referee report’s “replication” section, drafted in 30 minutes instead of 3 days.

title: Worked example — auditing a replication package
section: Direction B — building a package from your own project
text:
Direction B — building a package from your own project
You’ve got a paper accepted; the journal wants a replication package.

Step 1 — inventory what you actually used

“Look at every script in this project. List the ones that produce something cited in paper.tex (a number, a table, a figure). Anything not on that list is dead code or exploratory work that doesn’t belong in the public package.”



Step 2 — produce a clean structure

“Propose a folder structure for a public replication package: separate raw data, intermediate data, code, output. Don’t touch the files yet — just propose the layout.”

Approve the proposal.

“Now reorganize accordingly, copying (not moving) files from the current project into a new replication-package/ directory. Update path references in scripts so the package is self-contained.”







Warning



Have Claude copy, not move. Replication-package surgery is a one-way trip if you let it move things; you want your working project untouched until you’re sure the package builds.




Step 3 — pin the computational environment
A package that runs on your machine but nowhere else hasn’t been reproduced. Lock each language’s dependencies so a stranger gets the same versions you used.
R — renv. From the project root, snapshot exactly what the code uses:

“Set up renv for the R code: run renv::init(), make sure every library()/require() call resolves, then renv::snapshot() so renv.lock records exact package versions. Commit renv.lock and renv/activate.R.”

Julia — Project.toml + Manifest.toml. The Project.toml lists direct dependencies; the Manifest.toml is the exact-version lockfile.

“Make sure the Julia code runs under its own environment: a Project.toml with every package the code usings, and a committed Manifest.toml from Pkg.instantiate() so versions are pinned. Scripts should load it with --project.”

Stata has no lockfile, so record the version and list any non-base commands:

“Add version 18 at the top of each .do file, and write a code/00-install-deps.do that ssc installs every external command the package uses (esttab, reghdfe, etc.). Note the Stata flavor and version in the README.”

Commit all the lockfiles — they’re the difference between “should reproduce” and “does reproduce”.


Step 4 — write one script that runs everything
Tie it together with a single entry point that goes from a fresh clone to the finished tables and compiled paper, in order.

“Write a run_all.sh at the package root that, with set -euo pipefail and cd to its own directory, does this in order: (1) restore environments — renv::restore() for R and Pkg.instantiate() for Julia; (2) create the output directories (data/derived, output/tables, output/figures); (3) clean the raw data (Stata); (4) run the estimation (Julia); (5) build the LaTeX tables and figures (R), then compile paper/paper.tex. Print a one-line progress message before each stage; use relative paths.”

You’ll get something like:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "$0")"

echo "[1/5] Restoring environments..."
Rscript -e 'renv::restore(prompt = FALSE)'
julia --project -e 'using Pkg; Pkg.instantiate()'

echo "[2/5] Creating output directories..."
mkdir -p data/derived output/tables output/figures

echo "[3/5] Cleaning raw data (Stata)..."
stata-mp -b do code/01-clean.do

echo "[4/5] Estimating model (Julia)..."
julia --project code/02-estimate.jl

echo "[5/5] Building tables and compiling paper (R + LaTeX)..."
Rscript code/03-tables.R
( cd paper && latexmk -pdf paper.tex )

echo "Done. Tables in output/tables, paper at paper/paper.pdf."
Make it executable (chmod +x run_all.sh) and the whole package reproduces with one command: ./run_all.sh. That command is also exactly what the README’s “instructions to run” section should say.


Step 5 — write the README the way the AEA wants it

“Write a README.md for this replication package following the AEA data and code availability standards: data sources and access, computational requirements (software, packages, expected runtime), instructions to run, and a mapping from each table/figure in the paper to the script and output file that produces it.”

This README is the single most important document in your package. Read it critically — Claude can write a plausible-looking one that overstates how complete the package is.


Step 6 — confirm reproducibility on a fresh state

“Pretend you’ve never seen this project before. Following only the README, run ./run_all.sh from scratch. Stop and tell me if any stage is ambiguous, missing a dependency, or fails.”

This is the test you can’t easily run yourself — your machine has all your packages installed and your data sitting around. Claude can simulate the cold-start experience, and run_all.sh plus the committed lockfiles are what make that cold start actually work.

section: Why this is the highest-value use case
text:
Why this is the highest-value use case

Tedious. Every step is mechanical but requires care.
Error-prone for humans. Reading 40 files in order is exactly the task we’re worst at.
High stakes. A package that doesn’t reproduce is a paper that gets flagged by the data editor. A package with hardcoded paths is a paper that the field can’t build on.
Easy to verify. “Does it run on a fresh machine?” is a binary test. You’ll know if Claude’s audit was right.

title: Reorganizing a messy project before letting Claude Code work on it
text:
If you’re like most economists, your active research folders look something like this:
There is no README. The “live” version of paper.tex is in your head, not on disk. The Stata cleaning scripts call into Julia for estimation and R for figures, but nothing documents the order. Three of the .do files run; one runs but produces the wrong table; the other two break. The Julia files in estimate_test.jl are an old structural model; the live one is in estimate.jl. Two of the .dta files are inputs to something; the rest are dead. Half the scripts have hardcoded paths to your coauthor’s Dropbox folder.
This is fine for a human who wrote it. It is bad for Claude Code, which will read everything, get confused about which version is canonical, and either ask you a lot of questions or — worse — confidently edit the wrong file.
This page walks you through a one-time reorganization that gets the project into shape for agentic work. It is itself a perfect first project for Claude Code, because the agent can do most of the work and the worst case is recoverable.
crumbs: Reorganizing a messy project before letting Claude Code work on it

title: Reorganizing a messy project before letting Claude Code work on it
section: What “ready for Claude Code” actually means
text:
What “ready for Claude Code” actually means
You are aiming for a project where:

A stranger (or a future-you, or an RA, or Claude Code) can open the folder and figure out what’s going on within five minutes.
There is a single master script that runs every step from raw data to final tables and the compiled paper.
Live code is clearly distinguished from old/exploratory code. The archive is preserved, not deleted.
Every dependency between files is explicit (no hidden assumptions about what was last run by hand in Stata’s window).
A CLAUDE.md file at the root tells Claude what’s specific to your project: language version, conventions, what’s off-limits, where the data is, what the master script is.
A README.md tells a human reader the same things.
.gitignore keeps derived files and OS junk out of git.
Git is initialized so any change is recoverable.

A reasonable target structure (adjust to taste):
project-name/
├── README.md
├── CLAUDE.md
├── .gitignore
├── make-all.sh           (top-level orchestrator; calls each language in order)
├── data/
│   ├── raw/              (read-only; never modified by code)
│   └── derived/          (built from raw/ by code/)
├── code/
│   ├── 01-clean.do          (Stata: prep raw data)
│   ├── 02-estimate.jl       (Julia: structural estimation)
│   ├── 03-counterfactuals.jl (Julia: simulate)
│   └── 04-figures.R         (R: ggplot tables and figures)
├── output/
│   ├── tables/
│   └── figures/
├── paper/
│   ├── paper.tex
│   ├── references.bib
│   └── (figures, tables, etc.)
├── docs/                 (data dictionaries, notes, source docs)
└── archive/              (everything you didn't delete but isn't live)
The single code/ folder mixes Stata, Julia, and R because that’s how the work flows — the numeric prefixes (01-, 02-, …) make the order obvious regardless of language. Some people prefer code/stata/, code/julia/, code/r/ subfolders instead; either works as long as the orchestrator at the top knows the order.
This is a default, not a religion. AEA, TIER, BITSS, and the Reardon protocol all propose variations — pick one and stick to it.

title: Reorganizing a messy project before letting Claude Code work on it
text:
The walkthrough
Each step has the prompt you’d give Claude Code (in the integrated terminal of VS Code or in a bare terminal — your choice). Read every diff before approving.

Step 1 — Copy the project to a working directory
Do this in the terminal yourself, not through Claude. It is one command and it is the safety net for everything that follows.
cp -R ~/Dropbox/wage-paper ~/Desktop/wage-paper-cleanup
Or, on a Mac, use Finder: select the folder, Cmd-D to duplicate, move the duplicate somewhere outside Dropbox.






Tip



Already git-fluent and the original project is already in git? Use a worktree instead of cp -R.
cd ~/projects/wage-paper            # the original, already in git
git worktree add ../wage-paper-cleanup -b reorganize-2026
cd ../wage-paper-cleanup            # work here for the rest of this page
This replaces both Step 1 (copy) and Step 2 (git init + first commit). The worktree is a fresh working directory on its own branch, with the current main commit as the implicit baseline. You can skip ahead to Step 3.
A worktree gives you everything cp -R does, plus several real wins specific to a multi-step reorganization:

The reorganization is a reviewable change set. At the end, git diff main..reorganize-2026 shows the entire transformation as one diff you (and a coauthor, and Claude) can read.
Each step is its own commit on the branch. git log   reorganize-2026 is your audit trail. If a verification run fails three days from now, git bisect finds the exact commit that broke the result.
History stays connected to the original. Mid-reorganization, if a referee asks something about the published structure, cd   ~/projects/wage-paper and the original is right there, untouched and on main. With cp -R you’d have two disconnected copies and no easy way to compare.
Coauthor review before you commit to it. Push the branch; your coauthor reviews reorganize-2026 as a pull request and either approves the new structure or flags issues before you merge into main. A cp -R copy is invisible to them until you finish.
One-command cleanup if you abandon halfway: git worktree remove   ../wage-paper-cleanup && git branch -D reorganize-2026. Compared to rm -rf of a cp -R copy, this is the same outcome but with a paper trail in git reflog if you change your mind tomorrow.
The .gitignore you’ll write in Step 12 stays applied across reorganization steps automatically. No risk of accidentally committing build artifacts or derived data because the rules are inherited from the branch.

If you’re new to Git — or the original project isn’t yet in git — the cp -R path below is the recommended default. The full explanation of worktrees, with more use cases and pitfalls, is in the Worktrees section of the Git page.








Warning



Move the copy outside any cloud-synced folder (Dropbox, OneDrive, iCloud Drive). Reorganization will rename and move many files; you don’t want every intermediate state syncing across your devices and your coauthors’ machines. Once you’re done and verified, you can move the finished version back.
If your project contains IRB-protected, restricted-access, or otherwise confidential data, stop and read Confidential data before doing anything else. At minimum, make sure the data subfolder is not pulled into the working copy unless you’ve confirmed it’s safe to send to a cloud LLM provider in subsequent steps.


Verify the copy:
du -sh ~/Dropbox/wage-paper ~/Desktop/wage-paper-cleanup
Sizes should match within a few KB. Now cd into the copy and from this point on, work only there.
cd ~/Desktop/wage-paper-cleanup


Step 2 — Initialize git in the copy
Even if you never push to GitHub, local git is the recoverable history that makes the rest of this walkthrough safe. From inside the copy:
git init -b main
git add -A
git commit -m "Baseline before reorganization"
Now any change Claude makes is undoable with git checkout . or git reset --hard HEAD. This is the foundation of the “robust system with fail-safes” principle.






Tip



Never used Git? Read the Git page before this step. The five-minute version: Git takes snapshots of your project; every snapshot is permanent locally; you can always go back. Without Git, you have no fail-safe under what follows; with Git, every step on this page is one keystroke away from undoable.




Step 3 — Open Claude Code and take inventory
Start Claude in the copy:
claude
First prompt — purely read-only. You’re asking for a map, not an action:

“Read the entire project. Don’t modify anything. Produce a Markdown inventory with: (a) every top-level file and directory, (b) for each code file, a one-line description of what it appears to do, (c) for each data file, its size and a guess at whether it looks like raw input or derived output, (d) for each .tex file, whether it appears to be a paper draft, an old version, an appendix, slides, or something else. End with a section called ‘Open questions’ — things you’d need me to confirm before reorganizing.”

You will get back a 2-4 page document. Read it carefully. This is where you discover that analysis_v3_rebuttal.do is actually the live one and analysis.do is from two years ago — exactly the kind of thing a clean reorganization needs to get right.


Step 4 — Identify the live code path
Now narrow the inventory to what currently matters:

“Based on the inventory, identify the live code path — the minimal set of scripts and data files needed to reproduce the current version of paper.tex (or whichever .tex file I confirm is live). Trace dependencies: which scripts read which data files, which scripts produce which intermediate files, which scripts produce the tables and figures cited in the paper. Output as a Markdown list. Don’t move or delete anything yet.”

If Claude is unsure which .tex is the live paper, it will ask. Tell it.
What you get is a dependency map. Everything not on it is a candidate for archiving in step 6.






Warning



This is the step where Claude can hallucinate dependencies. Spot-check a few of its claims. Open a script Claude says produces Table 3; confirm it does. Open a .dta Claude says is unused; grep for its name across the project to make sure nothing references it. The cost of a hallucinated “this file is dead” is real — you might archive a file that something obscure actually needs.




Step 5 — Confirm and adjust the live path manually
This step is for you, not Claude. Read the dependency map. Add anything Claude missed. Remove anything you know is actually dead. The output of this step is your confirmed list of “what stays in the live path.”
A useful question to ask yourself for ambiguous files: “if this file went missing tomorrow, would I notice?” If no, archive. If yes, live.


Step 6 — Move exploration to archive/, don’t delete
Now the first real edit. Tell Claude:

“Create an archive/ directory. Move every file and folder NOT on the confirmed live-path list into archive/, preserving relative structure inside archive/ so I can find things later. Use git mv so the moves are tracked. Don’t delete anything. Show me the plan before executing.”

Use plan mode for this — Shift+Tab until you see “plan mode” before you send the prompt. You want to read the full move list before any file is touched.
When the moves are done, commit:
git add -A
git commit -m "Archive non-live files"






Tip



Why archive instead of delete? You will be wrong about what’s dead roughly 10% of the time. A coauthor will ask “what happened to the robustness check that used wage_no_outliers.dta?” and the answer “in archive/data/wage_no_outliers.dta” is much better than “I deleted it last Tuesday.”




Step 7 — Standardize the folder structure
Propose first, move second:

“I want to reorganize the live files into this structure: [paste the target structure from earlier on this page, edited for your project]. Propose how to map every current live file into the target structure. Don’t move anything yet. Flag any files where you’re not sure where they belong, and any files in the target structure that don’t exist yet (e.g., I have no master.do — that’s fine, we’ll create it later).”

Read the proposed mapping. Adjust anything that’s wrong. Then:

“Execute the mapping. Use git mv. Do not modify file contents — only move and rename. After every move, update path references in the remaining live files so the project still resolves. Cover each language’s idioms: Stata (include, do, use ... , clear, save, import delimited), R (source(), here::here(), readr::read_*(), setwd(), ggsave()), Julia (include(), using, CSV.read, joinpath(), Pkg.activate), Python (import, from ... import, pathlib.Path, pd.read_*, open()), LaTeX (\input{}, \includegraphics{}, \addbibresource{}), Matlab (addpath, cd, load, readtable). Show me each path-fix diff before applying.”

Plan mode again. Approve diffs one at a time. Commit when done:
git commit -am "Reorganize live files into standard structure"


Step 8 — Find and fix hardcoded paths

“Search the entire project (excluding archive/) for hardcoded absolute paths — anything starting with /Users/, /home/, C:\\, ~/Dropbox, or that references a specific user’s folder. List every occurrence with file and line number. Don’t change anything yet.”

You’ll get a list. For each hardcoded path, decide:

Convert to relative. Best default. /Users/me/Dropbox/wage-paper/data/raw.dta becomes data/raw/raw.dta.
Move to a config block. If the path points outside the project (a shared dataset on a research drive, say), put it in a small config.do (or config.R, etc.) at the project root and include it from each script. One place to change paths when machines change.
Document but leave alone. If the path is to a restricted-access data folder that genuinely lives elsewhere, document the requirement in the README and leave the path. Hardcoding is a feature here.

Then ask Claude to apply the conversion you decided:

“Convert paths in [list of files] from absolute to relative, assuming the project root is the working directory. Show diffs.”

Commit when done.


Step 9 — Draft CLAUDE.md
CLAUDE.md is read by Claude at the start of every session in this project. See Memory, CLAUDE.md, skills for the full picture; for now:

“Write a CLAUDE.md at the project root with: (1) one-paragraph description of what the project is and its current status, (2) the full stack — for every language used in code/, the version (Stata 18, R 4.4, Julia 1.11, Python 3.12, …) and the key packages, plus the LaTeX distribution and any Stata/R packages that aren’t on the default path, (3) folder conventions in this project (data/raw/ is read-only; output/ is built; etc.), (4) the orchestrator (make-all.sh or Makefile) and how to run it, including the order in which the languages are invoked and any language-specific gotchas (e.g., ‘the Stata binary on this machine is stata-mp’), (5) what to never do (don’t modify data/raw/, don’t commit data/derived/, don’t change paper/paper.tex without asking, etc.), (6) anything else a new collaborator would need. Read what’s already in the project to fill in real values; ask me where you’re unsure.”

Read what Claude produces. Edit it freely — this is your document. Commit.


Step 10 — Draft README.md
README.md is the human-facing version of CLAUDE.md, plus more context. Same principle: have Claude draft, you edit.

“Write a README.md at the project root following the AEA data and code availability standards: (1) project description and citation, (2) data availability and provenance — for each dataset in data/raw/, where it came from, whether it’s public or restricted, how to obtain it if restricted, (3) computational requirements — software, packages, expected runtime, (4) instructions to reproduce — exactly what command(s) someone runs from a clean clone, (5) a mapping from each table and figure in paper/paper.tex to the script and output file that produces it, (6) license. Use what’s already in CLAUDE.md and the code; ask me where you’re unsure.”







Warning



Read this draft critically. Claude can write a plausible-looking README that overstates how complete the project is. The data-availability section in particular: if your raw data came from a confidential source, say so explicitly and don’t let Claude paper over it.


Edit, commit.


Step 11 — Build a master script (the orchestrator)
If your project mixes languages — Stata cleaning, then Julia estimation, then R figures, then a LaTeX compile — no single language’s script can sit at the top. You want a language-agnostic orchestrator at the project root that calls each runner in order. A small shell script is the simplest answer; a Makefile is the upgrade path.
The prompt:

“Write a make-all.sh shell script at the project root that runs the full pipeline in order: invoke each language’s runner for the scripts in code/ (Stata for .do, Julia for .jl, R for .R, Python for .py if any), then compile paper/paper.tex. Use set -euo pipefail so the script halts on the first error. cd to the project root at the top so it works from anywhere. Print a one-line progress message before each step and a one-line success message at the end. Use relative paths.”

You’ll get something like:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "$0")"   # always run from project root

echo "[1/4] Cleaning data (Stata)..."
stata-mp -b do code/01-clean.do

echo "[2/4] Estimating model (Julia)..."
julia --project code/02-estimate.jl

echo "[3/4] Producing figures and tables (R)..."
Rscript code/04-figures.R

echo "[4/4] Compiling paper..."
( cd paper && latexmk -pdf paper.tex )

echo "Done. Outputs in output/, paper in paper/paper.pdf."
Make it executable once: chmod +x make-all.sh. From then on, one command rebuilds the whole project: ./make-all.sh.






Note



Single-language project? If everything is Stata, a master.do at the root that dos each script is fine. If everything is R, master.R calling source() on each script works. The orchestrator matters most when you cross language boundaries; below that, use what your language gives you.








Tip



A Makefile is the upgrade. Once your pipeline is stable and slow, a Makefile pays for itself: it re-runs only what’s downstream of the file you changed. For most econ projects you don’t need it on day one — but if a single rebuild starts taking 20+ minutes, that’s the signal to convert your make-all.sh into a Makefile with proper target: prerequisite rules.








Warning



Stata’s batch flag varies by platform and version. On Mac/Linux the typical invocation is stata-mp -b do script.do; on Windows it’s StataMP.exe /e do script.do. If your group uses Stata-SE or Stata-IC, the binary names differ (stata-se, stata). Tell Claude which binary you have in CLAUDE.md so it gets it right the first time.




Step 12 — Add .gitignore

“Write a .gitignore for this project. Exclude: (a) LaTeX build artifacts: *.aux, *.log, *.out, *.toc, *.blg, *.bbl, *.synctex.gz, *.fls, *.fdb_latexmk; (b) Stata: *.smcl log files (large; usually you only want the .log ASCII version); also Stata’s per-user temp files; (c) R: .Rhistory, .Rproj.user/, .Rdata, .RData; (d) Julia: *.cov. Decide whether to commit Manifest.toml: commit it if you want bit-exact reproducibility (recommended for replication packages); leave it ignored if you want package-version flexibility while you’re still developing; (e) Python: __pycache__/, *.pyc, .ipynb_checkpoints/, .venv/; (f) Matlab: *.asv (autosaves), *.mexmaci64, *.mexmaca64, *.mexa64, *.mexw64 (compiled MEX files); (g) OS junk: .DS_Store (macOS), Thumbs.db (Windows); (h) Derived data: data/derived/**; (i) Editor cruft: .vscode/ (unless you want to commit shared settings), .idea/. Show me the file before creating it.”

After it’s in place, clean up anything that’s already tracked but should be ignored:
git rm -r --cached data/derived
git commit -m "Stop tracking derived data"






Tip



One subtle Julia decision. Project.toml should always be committed — it lists which packages your code uses. Manifest.toml is the exact-version lockfile. For an active research project, ignoring Manifest.toml is fine (and keeps merge conflicts down with coauthors). For a replication package, commit it — readers should get the exact package versions you used.




Step 13 — Run end-to-end and verify
The whole point of the orchestrator and the clean structure is that you can do this:
# In the terminal, from the project root:
./make-all.sh        # or `make all` if you went the Makefile route
Or have Claude do it:

“Run ./make-all.sh from a fresh state. If any step errors, stop and tell me what happened — don’t try to auto-fix. After it succeeds, list every file produced under output/ and paper/, confirm the paper PDF compiled without unresolved references or missing-citation warnings, and report the total wall-clock runtime.”

If the master script doesn’t reproduce something that’s in your paper, that’s a real finding — either the live code path is wrong (re-do step 4) or there’s an undocumented manual step somewhere (document it in the README).
When everything runs end-to-end, commit:
git commit -am "Reorganization complete; master script reproduces all results"


Step 14 — Compare against the original
You worked in a copy. Before throwing away the original, do one final diff:

“List every table and figure file in the original project at ~/Dropbox/wage-paper/ (read-only — don’t modify anything there). For each, find the corresponding file in this reorganized project and compare. Flag any tables or figures that exist in the original but not here (might be missing live code), or that exist here but have different content (might be a numerical regression).”

Investigate any flags. When the diff is clean, the reorganized version is your new live project. Move it back to its permanent home (out of ~/Desktop/), update any external references, and you are done.

title: Reorganizing a messy project before letting Claude Code work on it
text:
Things to be careful about

Work in a copy, never on top of the original. The whole approach rests on this.
Archive, don’t delete. The cost of an over-aggressive archive is fishing a file out of archive/; the cost of an over-aggressive delete is rebuilding work from memory.
Some files look unused but aren’t. A .dta with no matching use might be loaded inside an included script, called from a Matlab routine, or read by a coauthor’s pipeline. Spot-check before archiving.
Talk to coauthors before reorganizing a shared project. A unilateral reorganization makes you the only person who can find anything for a month. Do it on a branch, share the new structure, then merge.
git mv preserves history but resets filesystem mtime. If anything you use depends on file timestamps, note it.
Confidential data is its own decision. If data/raw/ is restricted-access, was Claude reading it during the inventory step? If that’s not OK, move or symlink the data out before starting Claude. See Confidential data.

text:
When not to reorganize

Right before a deadline — the risk of silently breaking something outweighs the benefit.
For a project you’re about to abandon — just archive the whole folder.
Without a copy — see above.
On someone else’s published replication package — that’s a different workflow; see the replication-package audit.

A typical mid-sized project (one paper, 20–40 files, a few hundred MB) takes half a day to a full day the first time, most of it your own reading and judgment rather than waiting on Claude. It goes faster once the steps are familiar.

title: Git
text:
Git is the safety net that makes letting Claude Code edit your project tolerable. Without it, “Claude proposed a 200-line change across six files” is unnerving. With it, that’s just a yes/no decision: git checkout . to undo, or keep the change. One keystroke either way.
This page assumes you have never really used Git. If you have a GitHub account but only clone the odd repository, that counts as never.

title: Git
section: The mental model in two paragraphs
text:
The mental model in two paragraphs
Git is a time machine for a project folder. You decide when to take a snapshot — that’s a “commit.” Every commit is permanent, locally, forever. You can always come back to any past state. You don’t need to push to GitHub for any of this to work; “local Git” is enough to make the snapshots and the undo path.
Each commit has a short message (“fix Table 3 standard errors”), a date, an author, and a unique ID (a “hash” — a 7-character string like 8dad523). Commits form a chain. When you want to know what changed when, undo a change from yesterday, or see what your paper looked like three weeks ago, git has the answer.

title: Git
section: Why this matters for using Claude Code
text:
Why this matters for using Claude Code
Once an agent is editing your projects, Git earns its keep three ways:

Undoing. When Claude makes an edit you don’t like, git checkout --   file.tex puts the file back as it was at the last commit.
Reading the diff. Before accepting any non-trivial edit, you want to see exactly what changed. git diff shows you.
Recovering later. When you discover a week on that a refactor broke a result, git log and git checkout <past-hash> take you back.

Without Git, your fail-safe is “I have a backup somewhere?” — which isn’t one. This is the robust system the principles page describes, in concrete form.

title: Git
text:
Step 1 — Confirm Git is installed
On a Mac, Git ships pre-installed. In a terminal:
git --version
You should see something like git version 2.54.0. If not, the quickest fix is brew install git (if you have Homebrew) or downloading the installer from git-scm.com.
On Windows: install Git for Windows — it also gives you a usable bash terminal.

title: Git
section: Step 2 — Tell Git who you are (one-time setup)
text:
Step 2 — Tell Git who you are (one-time setup)
Git records who made each commit. Configure your name and email once, globally:
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@university.edu"
This is metadata, not authentication. It just labels your commits.
While you’re here, set the default branch name to main (the modern convention) and the default editor to something you can use:
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
git config --global core.editor "code --wait"   # if you use VS Code
# or "nano" if you'd rather not use VS Code as your git editor
You only do this once per machine.

title: Git
section: Step 3 — Initialize a Git repo in a project
text:
Step 3 — Initialize a Git repo in a project
cd into one of your project folders (one you’ve already reorganized — or any project you’d like a safety net under) and:
cd ~/Desktop/wage-paper
git init
That’s it. There’s now a hidden .git/ folder in your project that holds the entire history. You won’t ever look inside it.
Take the first snapshot, capturing the current state of everything:
git add -A
git commit -m "Initial commit"
Congratulations — you have a Git repository. There is now exactly one commit. Every change you make from this point on can be reviewed, diffed, and undone.






Tip



Run git init for every project, including teaching repos and side projects. It costs nothing and gives you the safety net everywhere. There is no downside to having a local-only Git history.

title: Git
text:
Step 4 — The daily loop
The cycle you’ll repeat constantly:
# 1. Work on your project (edit paper.tex, run analysis.do, whatever)

# 2. See what's changed since the last commit
git status

# 3. See the actual changes line-by-line
git diff

# 4. Decide what to commit. Either everything:
git add -A

# Or specific files:
git add paper.tex code/03-analysis.do

# 5. Take the snapshot
git commit -m "Update Table 3 with revised standard errors"
That’s the whole loop. Status → diff → add → commit. Do this several times a day, every day, on every project. Each commit is cheap and takes seconds.






Tip



Commit messages are notes to your future self. Treat them like the comment line at the top of a .do file. “Update results” is bad; “Fix Table 3 SE clustering at the firm level” is good. You’ll thank yourself when, six months later, you’re trying to figure out which commit broke the IV first stage.

title: Git
section: A first session, end to end
text:
A first session, end to end
Try this in any project:
cd ~/Desktop/some-project
git init
git add -A
git commit -m "Initial commit"

# Make a change — edit any file
echo "% added a comment" >> paper.tex

git status                    # tells you paper.tex is modified
git diff                      # shows the new line
git add paper.tex
git commit -m "Add a comment to paper.tex"

git log --oneline             # see your two commits
The whole thing takes two minutes. You now know enough Git to use it every day. Everything below is for the moments when something goes wrong — and those moments are when Git pays off most.

title: Git
text:
Reading the past
Once you have a few commits, the questions start: “what did this file look like last week?” “When did I change this?”
git log --oneline             # short list of every commit
git log paper.tex             # commits that touched paper.tex specifically
git show 8dad523              # the change made in commit 8dad523
git diff 8dad523              # diff against the state at commit 8dad523
git diff main~3 main          # diff between three commits ago and now
The ~3 notation means “three commits before”; main~3 is “three commits before the tip of main.” That’s the only weird syntax you’ll need for a while.

title: Git
text:
Undoing things — the safe operations
The five operations that cover almost every “oh no” moment:

Discard uncommitted changes to one file
You edited paper.tex, hated the result, want to go back to the last committed version:
git checkout -- paper.tex
Or, the modern equivalent (Git 2.23+):
git restore paper.tex
Either way, paper.tex is back to its last-committed state. The file you had on disk is gone.






Warning



This operation cannot be undone. The version on disk is overwritten. If the unsaved work mattered, you wanted to commit it (even on a “junk” branch) before discarding.




Discard ALL uncommitted changes
Same idea, broader. Wipes every uncommitted edit in the working tree:
git checkout .
Or:
git restore .
This is the canonical “Claude made a mess; start over from where I was” button.


Unstage a file (without losing changes)
You ran git add paper.tex but want to take it back without losing the edits:
git reset HEAD paper.tex
# or:
git restore --staged paper.tex
The file is no longer staged for the next commit, but your changes are still on disk.


See what a file looked like at a past commit
git show 8dad523:paper.tex > paper-from-may.tex
That writes the May version of paper.tex to a new file. You compare to the current one without disturbing anything.


Revert a single past commit
You committed 8dad523 last Tuesday and now want to undo just that change, without losing anything that came after:
git revert 8dad523
Git creates a new commit that’s the inverse of 8dad523. Safe; doesn’t rewrite history.

title: Git
text:
Undoing things — the destructive operations
These rewrite history. They’re sometimes the right tool, but they have sharp edges. Read carefully.






Warning



git reset --hard <hash> — moves the project back to the state at <hash> and discards every commit after it. Useful when you know the last few commits were a mistake; dangerous when you don’t.
git push --force — overwrites the remote branch with your local state, even if it diverges. Never do this on a shared branch without talking to coauthors first; it deletes their work from the remote.
git clean -fd — deletes every untracked file in the project. Useful when build artifacts are everywhere; dangerous because it can delete files Git has never seen and therefore cannot recover.








Tip



The safety net under the destructive operations: git reflog. Every state Git has ever been in is recorded in the “reflog” for 30 days, even after reset --hard. If you destroy work, the first thing to try is:
git reflog
That lists every state, with hashes. git checkout <hash> or git reset --hard <hash> brings you back. It’s the first thing to reach for when you think you’ve lost work.

title: Git
section: Branches — for trying things without breaking what works
text:
Branches — for trying things without breaking what works
Branches are alternate timelines. Useful for “let me try this big refactor without messing up the current paper draft.”
git checkout -b experiment        # create and switch to a new branch
# … work, commit, work, commit …
git checkout main                 # back to the main timeline
git merge experiment              # bring the experiment's commits into main
If you decide the experiment was a bad idea:
git checkout main
git branch -D experiment          # throw it away
For solo research projects, you’ll often skip branches entirely and just commit to main. That’s fine. Use branches when:

You want to try a structural change you might roll back.
You’re collaborating and want to share work-in-progress without disturbing the main line.
You’re preparing a replication package while still working on follow-ups.







Note



Merging is straightforward when nobody else has changed the same lines you did. When two people edit the same line, you get a “merge conflict” — Git asks you to choose between (or combine) the two versions. Don’t panic; this is a normal part of collaboration. Claude Code is good at walking you through resolving conflicts. See “When you’re stuck” below.

title: Git
section: Worktrees — when one working directory isn’t enough
text:
Worktrees — when one working directory isn’t enough
A worktree is a second (or third) working directory that shares the same .git repository. Each worktree sits on its own branch. You can edit, commit, run scripts in any worktree independently — but the underlying history is shared, so commits in one show up in the other the moment you pull or fetch.
This is not day-one Git. It is, however, the feature you’ll wish you had once you have a long-running project, coauthors, and Claude Code all in the same workflow.

The basic mechanics
From inside your existing project:
git worktree add ../paper-revision revision-2026
That creates a new directory at ../paper-revision, checked out on branch revision-2026 (created if it doesn’t exist). Your original working directory is unchanged — you can keep working in it. Open the new one in another VS Code window and you have two parallel checkouts of the same project.
When you’re done with the second worktree:
git worktree remove ../paper-revision
git branch -D revision-2026     # if you don't want to keep the branch


When you’d actually want this

Working on two branches without context-switching. You’re mid-revision on revision-2026 when a referee email arrives asking a quick question about a result on main. Without worktrees you’d git stash (which loses your editor state and any half-typed prompts to Claude), git checkout main, answer, switch back, git    stash pop. With worktrees: open the main worktree in another window, answer there, never disturb the revision work.
Long-running jobs you can’t interrupt. A Stata batch job is running in your project’s main checkout. Switching branches mid-job is risky — the script might pick up the wrong files partway through. A worktree on a different branch lets you do exploratory work in parallel without touching the running job.
Side-by-side comparison. Open the old version in one window, the new version in another. Especially useful for paper revisions: when you’re writing a response-to-referees, you can keep the submitted text and the revised text both on screen at once. Same trick for code: the published replication’s analysis.do in one window, your in-progress revision in another.
Reorganizing a project without copying. The reorganize-a-messy-project walkthrough recommends cp -R for git novices, but a worktree is a strict improvement when you’re git-fluent and the original is already in git. The reorganization shows up as a series of commits on a branch; git diff main..reorganize-2026 reviews the whole change at the end.
Letting Claude work in isolation. Claude Code’s Agent tool can spawn a sub-agent in its own worktree (the isolation: "worktree" option), so a disruptive task — a big refactor, a structural rewrite, an experimental rewrite of your tables — runs in a parallel checkout while you keep working in your main one. The agent reports back what it changed; you decide whether to merge. Without worktrees, the same task would either lock you out of your project for the duration or leave you wondering whether the agent’s half-finished state is corrupting what you’re looking at.
Multi-version verification. You want to confirm a result reproduces in both Stata 17 and Stata 18, or in both R 4.3 and R 4.4. A worktree per version with the relevant environment files committed lets you keep both setups warm at the same time.



Listing and pruning
git worktree list                  # show every worktree this repo has
git worktree prune                 # clean up stale references
git worktree list is the answer to “wait, did I create that other worktree six months ago and forget about it?”


Things to be careful about

Each worktree must be on a different branch. You can’t have two worktrees on main at the same time.
Don’t rm -rf a worktree folder. Use git worktree remove instead — otherwise Git keeps stale references and you’ll need to clean up with git worktree prune later.
Don’t put worktrees inside Dropbox / iCloud / OneDrive. Same sync-conflict reasons as putting your main project there.
Each worktree has its own untracked files. Things in .gitignore (build artifacts, derived data) are not shared between worktrees — each one builds its own.
Submodules and global git config are shared. Hooks, configured identity, etc., are repo-wide.

title: Git
text:
Going beyond your machine — GitHub
Everything above works with zero internet connection. Git is purely local. To back up your work, share with coauthors, or publish a replication package, you push to a “remote” — usually GitHub (github.com) but GitLab, Bitbucket, and self-hosted alternatives work the same way.

One-time setup per project
Create an empty repository on GitHub. It will give you a URL like https://github.com/yourname/wage-paper.git. In your local project:
git remote add origin https://github.com/yourname/wage-paper.git
git push -u origin main
The -u origin main part is shorthand for “remember that my local main corresponds to main on origin” — you only need it the first time.


The everyday loop, with a remote
When you’re working from one machine on a solo project, you don’t need to push every time. When you do push:
git push                    # send your commits to GitHub
git pull                    # fetch coauthors' commits and merge in
That’s the whole remote workflow. The vast majority of “Git frustration” in econ comes from forgetting to git pull before starting work — when you do, your commits and your coauthor’s commits diverge, and you have to do a merge.






Warning



Do not push your projects to a public GitHub repo without thinking about what’s in them. Anything in data/raw/ may include restricted-access or IRB-protected data. Anything in your code may include hardcoded paths revealing folder structures you’d rather not share. Default to private repos and only flip to public deliberately when you’re ready to publish a replication package. See Confidential data.

title: Git
text:
Coauthor workflow
Two coauthors editing the same project, each with their own laptop and a shared GitHub repo:

Always git pull before you start working. This brings their commits into your local copy.
Commit and push when you stop for the day. Tiny commits with real messages are infinitely better than one big “Update” commit at the end of the week.
If a git pull produces a merge conflict, Git will tell you exactly which files conflict. Open them; you’ll see markers like:
<<<<<<< HEAD
your version
=======
your coauthor's version
>>>>>>> main
Pick which one survives (or combine them), delete the markers, git add, git commit. Done.
Communicate before doing anything destructive on a shared branch. No git push --force, no git reset --hard of pushed commits, without a Slack/email/text first.

For most coauthorships, that’s it. You don’t need branches per collaborator unless the project gets complex.

title: Git
text:
What NOT to commit
A .gitignore file at the project root tells Git to skip these. The reorganize page’s Step 12 has a full template; the highlights:

Large data files. GitHub’s free tier limits files to 100 MB and repos to a soft 1 GB. For large datasets, use Git LFS or store the data outside the repo and document where it lives in the README.
Restricted-access or confidential data. Never commit it, full stop. See Confidential data.
Secrets / credentials. API keys, database passwords, anything ending in .pem or .key. If you ever commit one by accident, treat it as compromised and rotate it.
Derived outputs. data/derived/, output/tables/*.tex, paper/paper.pdf. These are reproducible from the source — no reason to track them.
Build artifacts. .aux, .log, .synctex.gz, *.smcl, __pycache__/, .Rhistory, etc.

title: Git
section: The friendly path: VS Code’s Source Control pane
text:
The friendly path: VS Code’s Source Control pane
If you’d rather use Git through a graphical interface, the best one is already inside VS Code. Open the Source Control pane (Ctrl+Shift+G or click the branching-tree icon in the left sidebar). You’ll see:

A list of every changed file, grouped by “Staged” and “Changes.”
Click any file to see the diff in the editor — same diff git diff prints, but pretty.
The + next to a file stages it. The - un-stages it.
The text box at the top is the commit message; the checkmark icon commits.
The … menu has push, pull, branch operations, etc.

If you’d rather not touch the CLI for Git, this is the recommended path. The same operations happen under the hood; you just click instead of typing. See the VS Code page for the broader VS Code setup.






Note



Other graphical Git clients worth knowing about: GitHub Desktop (simplest; free; opinionated), GitKraken (powerful; free for academic use), Sourcetree (free; aging). All are fine. If you’re already in VS Code, you don’t need any of them.

title: Git
section: What Claude Code does with Git on your behalf
text:
What Claude Code does with Git on your behalf
Claude Code knows Git. When working in a project with git init-d already, it will:

Run git status and git diff on its own to see what’s changed.
Stage and commit files when you ask.
Create branches if you ask.
Read history with git log to understand the project’s evolution.

It will not:

Run git push without you asking explicitly.
Run any destructive operation (reset --hard, clean -fd, push --force) without prompting first.
Commit changes silently. By default, you see what it staged before the commit happens.

A useful default is to let Claude commit on your behalf for routine work (“commit the bibliography fix you just made”), but type git push yourself the first time it goes to a shared remote. Pushes are visible to other people; that one’s worth a conscious keypress.

title: Git
text:
When you’re stuck
The “I think I broke Git” recovery path:

Stop. Don’t run more commands. The single most common way to make a Git problem worse is to keep running git commands hoping one of them fixes it.
Run git status and read what it says. Git’s error messages, for all their reputation, are usually accurate and tell you the next command to run.
git reflog is your “undo undo.” Every state Git has been in is recorded for 30 days. If you destroyed something, it’s almost certainly in there. Find the hash you want; git checkout <hash> to inspect, git reset --hard <hash> to fully restore.
Ask Claude. Open Claude Code in the project, paste the output of git status and git reflog, and say what you were trying to do when things went wrong. Claude is genuinely good at Git diagnosis — it’s seen every variation of “I made a mess” before.

title: Git
text:
What you can safely skip
Rebase, cherry-pick, stash, submodules, and hooks are all real tools, but none are on your critical path for econ research — pick them up the day you actually need one. The Pro Git book covers them when you’re ready. The one to keep at arm’s length is git push --force on a shared branch: it can delete coauthors’ commits, so never run it without a talked-through agreement (and prefer git push --force-with-lease, which refuses to overwrite work you didn’t know about).

title: Git
text:
Where to go next

Verifying output — many of the verification habits (“commit before any big change”) become trivial once Git is in your fingers.
Principles — Git is the second principle (“a robust system with fail-safes”) in concrete form.

What: Claude reads the relevant files, thinks about the change, and writes a plan for your approval before touching anything.

title: What you must still do yourself
text:
The list

Specification
What’s the right model? What controls? What functional form? What sample restriction? Claude can implement any of these; it cannot tell you which is correct for your question.


Identification
Why does this design recover a causal effect? What threats remain? What robustness checks address them? The model can list textbook threats; it cannot judge whether your setting has them.


Interpretation
What does the coefficient mean? Is it economically large? Is it consistent with prior estimates? What’s the policy or theoretical takeaway? Claude can produce confident-sounding interpretations that are wrong about your context.


Contribution
What’s new here? Why should anyone care? Where does this sit in the literature? Claude has read a lot but has no taste — it cannot tell you whether your contribution is interesting.


Authorship
Anything you submit goes out under your name. Claude is a tool — don’t list it as a co-author, don’t pretend it didn’t help, and disclose LLM use as your journal requires.


The hard problem
The model is good enough that you’ll be tempted to outsource judgment disguised as code: “write the empirical strategy section”, “decide which controls to include”, “write the limitations section”. Notice when you’re about to do this. The cost of bad judgment doesn’t go down because the typing got faster.

title: LLMs for Economists
text:
A field guide to one specific way of using LLMs: giving an AI agent direct access to your project files so it can write code, edit your LaTeX, audit a replication package, and run things on your behalf — under your supervision.
Chat tools — ChatGPT or Claude in a browser — are handy for quick questions. Agentic coding is the bigger change of the last year, and it’s what this guide covers.

title: LLMs for Economists
text:
Suggested reading order
If you have 30 minutes:

What is agentic coding? — what it means and why it’s different from chatting with an LLM (five minutes).
Install Claude Code, then use it inside VS Code — recommended if you’re coming from RStudio, Stata, or Matlab. (Never used the terminal? The terminal primer is helpful background even on the VS Code route.)
A worked example: editing a LaTeX paper or auditing a replication package.

If you have a free afternoon, add:

Plan mode, todos, slash commands.
The example page for your language: Stata, R, or Julia.
How to ask and verifying output — how to ask well and when to check the result.
The pitfalls, before letting Claude touch anything serious: confidential data, hallucinations, and what you must still do yourself.

Work in progress
The two long-form examples (LaTeX paper editing and replication-package audit), the install guide, and the Git and terminal primers are the most complete pages. Others are short outlines for now. If a section would help you and isn’t there yet, email me — that’s the fastest way to set the priority.

title: Principles
text:
So I thought I will put my thoughts in here after our department meeting with the help of Claude Code. Most of this is based on my experience of using chatbot AI and agentic AI. So most of my thoughts are based on my usage of LLM products from Anthropic (Claude, Claude Code), OpenAI (Chat GPT, Codex) and a little of Github (Github copilot). I use Claude most of the times. The efficiency gains that can be had depends heavily on how our workflow is aligned with how large language models (LLMs) work.
The difference between chatbot AI tools like Claude (and Chat GPT) and agentic AI like Claude code (and Codex) is that in the former you are in a chat session and in the latter the AI does stuff on your behalf and uses your computer to implement stuff using Bash scripts, after you give it directory level permissions to run things. The major efficiency gains come from using agentic AI over chatbot AI. In the latter there is a wide variety of how much you let your LLM do your work. I used to think that this depends on how risk averse you are. But in my experience, I think it more depends on how detailed your prompting is such that the LLM understands the context, how robust your system such that it has fail-safes, and how do you design your workflow so that the agent can verify its own work and can hence iterate on its mistakes minimizing your intervention.
The rest of this page expands on those three things, because they are what I would have wanted someone to tell me a year ago.

title: Principles
text:
1. Detailed prompting and context
The single biggest predictor of whether Claude Code does something useful on the first try is whether I gave it enough context to understand what I actually want. “Detailed prompting” means giving the model the information a smart RA would need to do the job — the relevant files, the constraints, the goal. Length has nothing to do with it.
In practice, this is three things:

Name the files. “Read paper.tex and tell me…” beats “look at my paper” every time. The model can find files; it cannot read your mind about which one you mean.
State the constraint, not just the goal. “Reformat all my tables using booktabs” is the goal. “Reformat all my tables using booktabs; do not change any numbers, captions, or column headers” is the constraint that prevents Claude from “tidying up” content you didn’t ask it to tidy.
Provide stable context once, not every session. A CLAUDE.md file at the root of your project — saying which Stata version you use, which scripts produce which outputs, what’s off-limits — is read at the start of every session. Writing it once saves you re-explaining. See Memory, CLAUDE.md, skills.

The mental model that helped me: a chatbot prompt is a Google query, but an agentic prompt is a memo to a new RA on day one. Different audience, different register.
What this looks like in our examples:

The first paragraph of every prompt in the LaTeX paper walkthrough is an orientation pass — having Claude read the project before doing anything.
The replication-package audit starts by asking Claude to describe the dependency map before changing anything. The audit is the context for the action.

title: Principles
text:
2. A robust system with fail-safes
This was the principle that took me longest to internalize because it requires admitting up front that the model will sometimes do the wrong thing — and designing your environment so a wrong action is recoverable rather than catastrophic.
The fail-safes I rely on are not exotic:

Git, even just locally. I commit before any non-trivial change. If Claude makes an edit I don’t like, git checkout . undoes everything in the working directory. You don’t need to push to GitHub for this to save you. (New to Git? The Git page is the shortest path from zero to using it as a daily safety net.)
Plan mode. For any change touching multiple files, I hit Shift+Tab until the prompt says “plan mode”. Claude reads, thinks, and writes a plan for my approval. I read the plan; if it misunderstands, I correct before any file is touched. See Plan mode, todos, slash commands.
Don’t blanket-allow destructive operations. Claude Code prompts before things like deleting files, force-pushing to git, or running rm -rf. Don’t override those prompts. The two-second pause is the difference between a recoverable mistake and a Saturday spent reconstructing your project from memory.
A working “master script” in every project. A single master.do, master.R, or make all that rebuilds your results from scratch. After any meaningful change, ask Claude to re-run it and confirm outputs match. This is your reproducibility check and your fail-safe.
Read-only patterns for restricted data. When I work on projects with IRB-protected or restricted-access data, Claude only ever sees the code, never the data. The data lives in a folder Claude is not pointed at. See Confidential data.

A useful test: before starting a task, ask yourself “if Claude does the worst plausible thing here, what is my recovery?” If the answer is “git checkout”, you’re fine. If the answer is “rebuild from backups” or “email my coauthor”, slow down and add a fail-safe first.

title: Principles
section: 3. A workflow the agent can verify on its own
text:
3. A workflow the agent can verify on its own
This is the principle with the highest payoff and the one most colleagues miss: structure the task so the agent can check its own work, and it can iterate on its mistakes without needing you in the loop for every step.
A few examples of what this looks like in econ work:

Replication. “Re-run master.do and tell me whether each table in output/tables/ matches the version checked into git.” The agent runs the script, diffs the outputs, and either reports “all match” or “Table 3 changed — here’s the diff”. One human-readable status; no per-step babysitting.
Cleaning. Add assertions to your cleaning scripts: assert wage > 0 if inrange(year, 2000, 2020). When Claude edits the cleaning code and an assertion fails, the script halts and the agent sees exactly what broke. It can iterate to fix the bug without you.
LaTeX. After every edit to a .tex file, Claude can compile and read the log. Unresolved references, overfull boxes, missing citations — all surface immediately, and the agent can either fix them or escalate to you.
Numerical work. A test that checks the sign and rough magnitude of the main coefficient (not its exact value) is enough for Claude to notice when a refactor silently breaks the analysis.
Code review. For non-trivial edits I ask Claude to run /review on its own diff before showing it to me. It catches its own clumsy edits about half the time.

When this principle is in place, my supervision shifts from “every keystroke” to “every milestone”. I check in when the agent reports something done, not while it works.

title: Principles
text:
Putting it together
These three principles compound. Detailed prompting is wasted if the agent can’t recover from a wrong turn. Fail-safes keep you safe but not productive. Self-verification is impossible without context to verify against. Roughly:

efficiency ≈ (quality of context) × (recoverability of the system) × (degree to which the agent can check its own work)

If any factor is near zero, the product is too — the model being capable doesn’t help. Most of my own learning has been about raising the third factor: the model is capable enough; the bottleneck was giving it the scaffolding to work without me hovering over it.

title: Principles
text:
Where to go from here

The most concrete application of all three principles at once is reorganizing a messy project — context (a fresh inventory), recoverability (a copy plus git), and self-verification (a master script the agent can re-run) are all built into the walkthrough.
See these principles applied end-to-end in the replication-package audit and the LaTeX paper walkthrough.
For the operational habits — what to type, what to leave alone, when to hit plan mode — see How to ask and Verifying output.
For what these principles don’t protect you from — research judgment, identification, interpretation — see What you must still do.

title: Hallucinations
text:
Warning



Coming soon. A field guide to the specific kinds of hallucinations that hurt empirical economists, and the verification habits that catch each one.

title: Hallucinations
text:
What gets hallucinated

1. Citations and references

Bibliography entries that don’t exist.
Cited claims that the paper doesn’t actually make.
Slightly wrong years, page numbers, or author orders.

Catch: before any new \cite{...} lands in your paper, open the source paper and confirm.


2. Regression results

Coefficients reported without the regression having actually been run.
“I ran your model and got…” when no Bash tool call was made.

Catch: re-run the regression yourself, or insist Claude show you the log/output from a real run.


3. Function and option names

A Stata command that doesn’t exist, or has a different syntax than Claude reports.
An R function from the wrong package, or with arguments that don’t exist.
A LaTeX package that doesn’t behave the way Claude described.

Catch: for unfamiliar commands, check the documentation. For Stata: help <command>. For R: ?fn or the package’s website.


4. File contents

A claim about what’s in a file that Claude didn’t actually read.

Catch: Claude shows you tool calls. If it claims to have looked at paper.tex but you don’t see a Read tool call for it, push back: “Did you actually read it? Show me.”


5. Replication-package completeness

“I ran the master script and everything worked” when it didn’t.
“All your tables are reproduced” without checking.

Catch: diff the produced output against what’s in your paper.

title: Hallucinations
text:
The general rule
Claude states wrong answers as confidently as right ones. Treat its output the way you’d treat a draft from a new RA on day one: usefully, and with full verification.
